one_liner: Linux one-loop-per-thread C++ TCP reactor library; author's ping-pong test puts it about 18% above libevent2's bufferevents.
what_it_does: Muduo is an event-driven TCP networking library for multi-threaded Linux servers: an EventLoop (one epoll/poll reactor per thread), TcpServer/TcpClient with callback-style connection and message handlers, a growable Buffer, timers, and an EventLoopThreadPool that assigns connections round-robin to I/O threads. It is not a drop-in for libevent; you write C++ callbacks (std::function) against muduo's own classes. A minimal HttpServer in muduo/net/http and many protocol examples (pingpong, ttcp, memcached, protorpc, socks4a) ship with it.
how_it_is_fast: Reads go through Buffer::readFd, a single readv into the buffer's free space plus a 64 KiB stack buffer, so one syscall drains up to about 128 KiB without an ioctl(FIONREAD); libevent 2.0.21 and 2.1.12 evbuffer_read issue FIONREAD and cap every read at EVBUFFER_MAX_READ = 4096 bytes. Sends try a direct write() when the output buffer is empty and only queue the remainder; each connection is pinned to one I/O thread, so the hot path takes no locks. Built with -O2 -march=native by default.
when_to_use: Custom binary or line-based TCP protocol servers on Linux (RPC, gateways, game or chat servers) where you want a small, readable reactor rather than a full web framework.
Throughput-bound echo/relay/proxy workloads with message sizes of a few KiB and up, where the larger reads beat libevent bufferevents' 4 KiB-per-read path.
Multi-core servers that fit the one-loop-per-thread model: set TcpServer::setThreadNum(N) and keep per-connection state in the owning loop.
Teaching or vendoring: BSD-3-Clause, small C++11 codebase, documented in the author's book on Linux multithreaded server programming.
when_not_to_use: HTTP services: the bundled HttpServer parses request line and headers only; the kExpectBody branch in HttpContext.cc is an empty FIXME, so request bodies (POST) and chunked encoding are not handled. Use Drogon or Sogou Workflow for HTTP.
Windows, macOS or BSD targets: Linux-only (epoll, timerfd, eventfd; kernel >= 2.6.28).
Projects that need TLS, HTTP/2, coroutines or async DNS out of the box: none are in the core library (c-ares, curl, hiredis and protobuf appear only in examples/contrib).

Long-term-supported dependencies: last code change 2022-11-01, 41 open issues and 45 open PRs, no tagged GitHub releases; open bugs include timer callbacks still running after cancel (#668) and a stack overflow in TimeZone::loadZoneFile on a crafted zone file (#728).

integration.form: static lib (CMake or Bazel; libmuduo_base and libmuduo_net, optional muduo_http)
integration.dependencies: Boost headers (boost::any only); pthreads; examples optionally use protobuf, zlib, c-ares, curl, hiredis, thrift, gd, tcmalloc
integration.platforms: Linux only (kernel >= 2.6.28), any architecture GCC targets; default flags include -march=native
integration.thread_safety: One EventLoop per thread; EventLoop::runInLoop/queueInLoop/quit and TcpConnection::send are safe from other threads (cross-thread send copies the data); TcpConnection::shutdown, TcpServer setters and HttpServer::setHttpCallback are documented as not thread safe.

gotchas: Harness note on the 18% claim: each side is measured with its own client and server (chenshuo/recipes pingpong/libevent vs muduo examples/pingpong, the scripts default to 16 KiB blocks, server and client pinned to separate cores with taskset). The libevent side runs on bufferevents, whose evbuffer_read caps each read at 4096 bytes after an ioctl(FIONREAD) (libevent 2.0.21 buffer.c, unchanged in 2.1.12), so a 16 KiB message costs libevent at least four read callbacks per hop versus one readv for muduo. The gap measures that default buffer path, not the epoll loop; evpp's docs say evpp beats libevent2 for the same reason (it uses libevent's event loop but its own muduo-style Buffer instead of evbuffer).

CMakeLists.txt compiles with -Werror plus -Wconversion, -Wold-style-cast and -Wshadow, and with -march=native; new compilers can stop the build on fresh warnings, and binaries are not portable across CPUs unless you remove -march=native. build.sh defaults to an out-of-tree ../build directory.

TcpConnection::send(Buffer*) is commented 'this one will swap data' but copies: in-loop it writes or appends from the buffer and then retrieveAll(); from another thread it copies into a std::string first.
Buffer::readFd uses a 64 KiB stack array on every read callback, so I/O threads need a normal-size stack; Buffer is backed by std::vector<char> and never shrinks unless you call shrink().
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick muduo over Drogon, Sogou Workflow or cinatra when you are writing a raw TCP protocol server, not an HTTP API, and want a small Linux reactor you can read end to end; for HTTP serving those siblings are complete frameworks with published HTTP benchmarks, while muduo's HttpServer has no request-body support.
verified_claims_summary: The muduo author's 2010 CSDN post (not reachable here; quoted by Qihoo360's evpp docs) reports muduo ping-pong echo throughput on loopback averaging more than 18% above libevent 2.0.x across message sizes and connection counts; hardware, compiler and per-row numbers are not verifiable. The public harness builds the libevent test programs with -g -Wall -O2 against an installed libevent, while muduo's current CMake release build uses -O2 -march=native. Evpp's separate run (Xeon E5-2630 v2, gcc 4.8.2) shows muduo-v1.0.9 roughly equal to evpp-v0.2.4, which is itself 17% to 130% faster than libevent-2.0.21's samples, so the 18% is indirectly plausible but never measured by a third party.
status_note: Stale: the last code commit is 2022-11-01 (the 2025-02-28 commit is an issue-template update) and there are no tagged GitHub releases, but it is BSD-3-Clause, widely forked (16.3k stars, 5.3k forks) and small enough to vendor; the issue #720 reporter built it with gcc 13.3 once the distro Boost replaced a self-built one.
